Devin Desktop + CLI walkthrough · Booz Allen edition

Ship a Coverage Gap report in MITRE ATT&CK Navigator with Devin Desktop

  • Audience: Booz Allen engineers who have completed the Devin Desktop 101 / 201 and Devin CLI 101 sessions and want to practise on a real codebase.
  • Repo: mitre-attack/attack-navigator, the ATT&CK Navigator (Angular, TypeScript, Angular Material, Karma/Jasmine), master branch. MITRE's open-source tool for annotating ATT&CK matrices, used by SOCs, red teams and threat-intel analysts.
  • You need: only Devin Desktop and the Devin CLI (FedRAMP builds from windsurf.fedstart.com/install; no Devin yet? request access through the Booz Allen service desk). Node.js is the only other requirement, and Part 0 covers it. There is no Docker, database, account or API key involved.
  • Docs: Devin Desktop · Devin Local agent · Devin CLI · Federal
  • Time: about 1¾ hours for Parts 0–5 (Part 0 is around 15 minutes, mostly waiting on npm ci). Part 6 is an optional 30–45 minute stretch.

Goal. You will add a Coverage Gap report to ATT&CK Navigator: a sidebar panel that shows, for the current layer, how many techniques in each tactic you have annotated (scored, commented or tagged with metadata), lists the ones you have not, and exports the result as CSV. Detection-engineering and purple-team leads ask this question of every layer (“where are our gaps?”), and today they answer it by looking at the colours. The change touches a calculation on the view model, a new Angular component, sidebar and toolbar wiring, a feature flag in config.json and tests, and you can see it working in a browser at the end.

Along the way you will use the Devin Desktop features available in the FedRAMP boundary that come up in daily work (DeepWiki, Codemaps, Tab, the Devin Local agent in Ask, Plan and Code modes, permission modes, context from @-mentions, images and terminal output, AGENTS.md, Skills), then repeat part of the workflow from the Devin CLI.

The parts follow the order you would work in, not the order of the slide decks. Each is tagged with the session it draws on:

How to read this page. Prompt cards are what you type into the Devin Local agent in Devin Desktop; CLI cards are for the terminal. Each prompt card names the mode to be in when you send it. Every card and code block has a one-click Copy. Checkpoints have a checkbox you can tick as you go. The first mention of each concept links to the matching section of the Devin docs.

Two habits this lab drills.

1. Start in Plan mode. For anything beyond a one-line fix, begin in Plan mode. The agent reads the code without editing, writes a plan and asks for approval. Read it, push back where needed, then approve, and the agent moves on to implementing in Code mode (type /normal if it does not switch on its own). Reviewing an approach is cheaper than reviewing a diff. Ask mode is for questions only. Starting in Code mode is fine for tasks that are already obvious.

2. The prompts here are over-specified on purpose. A group needs everyone to land on the same result, so many cards spell out file names, commands and edge cases. In daily work you can say much less. “Add a per-tactic coverage report to the sidebar, like layer settings” is a fine opening in Plan mode; the agent will find the patterns and ask about what it cannot infer. Where it helps, cards include a Looser version showing how little you need to type.

Part 0 — Set up from a bare machine Desktop 101CLI 101~15 min

This part assumes nothing is on your machine except Devin Desktop and the Devin CLI. Besides getting Navigator running, it shows that “set up my environment” is a task you can hand to the agent. Navigator was chosen for this lab partly because setup is short: it is a client-side Angular app that reads ATT&CK data over HTTPS and keeps layers in the browser, so there is no database, container runtime or login.

0.1 — Install Devin Desktop and the Devin CLI (FedRAMP)

Don’t have Devin yet? Booz Allen staff request Devin access through the internal service desk: Request Devin access (BAH service desk). That request covers Devin only. Node.js and Git go through your normal software-request channel (0.2).

  • Devin Desktop: windsurf.fedstart.com/install. Pick your platform, install, and sign in with your organisation account (set-up and onboarding steps). If Devin Desktop is not offered for your account, your internal Devin POC can enable it.
  • Devin CLI: windsurf.fedstart.com/install/cli. You will not use it until Part 6, but install it now. The two share AGENTS.md and Skills, and Part 6 depends on that.

Open Devin Desktop. The agent panel is on the right side of the IDE. Check the agent selector in the bottom-right corner says Devin Local. That is the agent used throughout this walkthrough; it shares its harness, modes, Skills and permission model with the CLI. If it is not listed, follow the agent settings steps or ask your admin to enable it.

0.2 — Get Node.js and Git (no package managers)

Navigator needs one runtime, Node.js 22, which includes npm and npx. You also need Git to clone. On a managed Booz Allen machine, assume Homebrew, winget, Chocolatey and similar package managers are not available, and use the vendor installers through your approved software channel:

  • Node.js 22 (LTS): the installer from nodejs.org/en/download for your OS. Request it the way you request any software. Version 22 is what Navigator’s README calls for; a newer LTS will normally work too.
  • Git: macOS ships it with the Xcode Command Line Tools; on Windows request Git for Windows; on Linux it is in the distro repos.

Whatever you already have, let the agent audit the machine first. Open an empty folder in Devin Desktop (File → Open Folder, then make a repos folder) and start in Plan mode, as you will for every task in this lab:

Prompt Plan mode → Code mode · Normal permissions
Check whether git and Node.js 22 (with npm) are installed and working on this machine — run `git --version`, `node --version` and `npm --version`. I'm on a managed corporate laptop: no Homebrew, winget or other package managers. For anything missing or the wrong major version, write a plan that uses only the official installers (nodejs.org, Git for Windows or Xcode CLT) or tells me exactly what to request from IT, and includes the post-install checks. Don't install anything until I approve the plan.

Read the plan, approve it, and the agent moves into implementation. Two things to notice. In Normal permission mode, every shell command shows up as a permission card you approve, edit or reject; read them, because they are the safety model. And the agent adapts to your OS: on Windows it will check that node is on the PATH of a new terminal, and on macOS it may point out that the Node installer needs admin rights.

Corporate machines. If the agent hits an admin-rights or proxy wall it cannot work around, it should stop and ask you. Get the installer through your software channel, then come back and re-run the version checks. If npm ci in 0.4 fails with a certificate or proxy error, ask your IT contact for the standard npm config proxy and CA settings for your network instead of disabling TLS checks.

0.3 — Clone Navigator

Ask the agent to do it, or run this in the built-in terminal (Terminal → New Terminal, or Ctrl+`):

git clone https://github.com/mitre-attack/attack-navigator.git
cd attack-navigator
git checkout -b feature/coverage-gap-report

Then File → Open Folder → the attack-navigator directory, so Devin Desktop’s indexing, DeepWiki and Codemaps are scoped to this repo. Open a fresh agent conversation there.

0.4 — Install dependencies and start the app

The Angular application lives in nav-app/. The repo root holds the README, USAGE.md, sample layers/ and Dockerfiles you will not use. Let the agent do the setup in Plan mode, so you can see it read the README before touching anything:

Prompt Plan mode → approve → Code mode
Set this repo up for local development without Docker. Read README.md and nav-app/package.json, then plan: install dependencies in nav-app with `npm ci` (not `npm install` — keep package-lock.json unchanged), start the dev server with `npx ng serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 4200` in a terminal I can keep open, confirm http://localhost:4200/ returns the app, and tell me which npm scripts exist for tests, lint and formatting. Don't modify any tracked files.

Looser version (what you would type in practice, in Plan mode): “Get this running locally and tell me how to run the tests. Plan first.” The agent will read the README itself. The npm ci versus npm install point is the kind of convention you catch when you read the plan.

Or run it yourself:

cd nav-app
npm ci                                        # 2–5 min the first time
npx ng serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 4200       # leave this terminal running

The app comes up at http://localhost:4200 once the terminal prints Compiled successfully. The first compile takes 20–40 seconds. Angular’s dev server watches the source tree, so later edits by you or the agent show up in the browser on save.

Why npm ci? It installs what package-lock.json pins and fails if the lock file is out of sync, where npm install would rewrite it. In a shared repo that is the difference between “works on my machine” and a reproducible setup, and it is the first thing worth writing into AGENTS.md in Part 3.

0.5 — Open a layer

Open http://localhost:4200. On the landing tab choose Create New Layer → Enterprise ATT&CK. Navigator fetches the current ATT&CK Enterprise data from MITRE’s public STIX feed (the one network call the app makes) and renders the matrix: 14 tactic columns, 200-plus techniques, and sub-technique counts like (0/4) under each. The toolbar at the top right has three tabs: Selection Controls, Layer Controls and Technique Controls. This is your start state, and the path you will verify against in Part 5.

What you do not need. No login, API key or database. Layers live in the browser tab until you download them as JSON (Layer Controls → download). If your network blocks raw.githubusercontent.com, the matrix will stay empty; the FAQ explains how to point Navigator at a local copy of the ATT&CK data.

0.6 — Agent-config files you will create in this lab

Navigator ships without an AGENTS.md or any Skills (it has a CONTRIBUTING.md written for people), so you will create them the way you would on your own project:

  • AGENTS.md (repo root): always-on rules covering overview, exact commands, conventions and boundaries. Part 3.1.
  • .devin/skills/navigator-feature-checklist/SKILL.md: the repo’s quality gate as an on-demand procedure. Part 4.1, modified in 4.2.
  • .devin/skills/layer-format-review/SKILL.md: a second, narrower Skill. Part 4.3.

Devin Local and the Devin CLI share a harness, so the same files drive both. Part 6 shows this.

Part 1 — Understand Navigator Desktop 101Desktop 201~15 min

ATT&CK Navigator is MITRE’s open-source web app for annotating ATT&CK matrices. Analysts colour, score and comment techniques to show detection coverage, red-team plans or threat-actor behaviour, and save the result as a layer (JSON). It is a single Angular application under nav-app/, organised by role rather than by feature:

nav-app/src/app/ ├── classes/ the model layer — plain TypeScript, no Angular │ ├── stix/ Domain, Matrix, Tactic, Technique (parsed ATT&CK STIX data) │ ├── view-model.ts ViewModel = one layer: name, filters, gradient, and a TechniqueVM per technique │ ├── technique-vm.ts TechniqueVM = one technique's annotations (score, comment, metadata, links…) │ └── index.ts barrel export ├── services/ DataService (loads STIX), ConfigService (assets/config.json), ViewModelsService ├── datatable/ the toolbar: Selection / Layer / Technique controls ├── sidebar/ the right-hand panel; switches on viewModel.sidebarContentType ├── layer-settings/ one sidebar panel (a standalone component) — your template ├── search-and-multiselect/, layer-upgrade/ … other sidebar panels ├── matrix/ the matrix rendering └── *.spec.ts colocated Karma/Jasmine tests at every layer nav-app/src/assets/config.json ← feature flags for every toolbar control (features → layer_controls → …)

You are going to add a new sidebar panel down that stack: a calculation on ViewModel, a standalone component that renders it, a branch in the sidebar, a button in Layer Controls and a feature flag. Before planning anything, build a mental model with the three “understand” tools from Desktop 101.

1.1 — DeepWiki: explain what you are looking at

DeepWiki shows explanations of functions, classes and files inside the editor. Open nav-app/src/app/classes/technique-vm.ts, hover the TechniqueVM class and then its annotated() method, and read the explanation. Annotated means the technique has a score, comment, links or metadata, which is the definition of “covered” your report will use. Then do the same for Tactic in classes/stix/tactic.ts. Its constructor filters out revoked and deprecated techniques, so anything iterating tactic.techniques already gets a clean list.

1.2 — Codemaps: see the flow end to end

Codemaps turn a question into a written and visual map of the relevant code that you can click through. Open the Codemaps view and submit:

Codemap prompt
Trace what happens when a user clicks the "layer settings" button in the Layer Controls toolbar: from the button in the datatable component, through the ViewModel's sidebar state, to the sidebar component deciding which panel to render, to the LayerSettingsComponent and how it reads and writes the ViewModel. Also show how config.json feature flags decide whether the button is displayed at all.

Click through the nodes. You should land on data-table.component.html (a control-row-item guarded by configService.getFeature(...) and isControlIncluded('layer_controls', …)) → openLayerSettings() in data-table.component.ts → viewModel.sidebarContentType / sidebarOpened → the *ngIf chain in sidebar.component.html → <app-layer-settings [viewModel]=…>. Your Coverage Gap panel will copy that five-hop chain. Keep the Codemap open; you can reference it when prompting.

1.3 — Tab: inline completion

Open nav-app/src/app/classes/view-model.ts and find sidebarContentTypes = ['layerUpgrade', 'search', 'layerSettings']. Put the cursor after 'layerSettings', type , 'cov and watch Tab propose the completion. Press Tab to accept, then undo. The agent will make this edit properly in Part 3; the point here is the difference between Tab (inline, keystroke-level) and the agent (multi-file, task-level).

1.4 — Add context deliberately

The agent finds context on its own and does better with your guidance. Three ways you will use in this lab:

  • @-mention files and folders in the prompt (@nav-app/src/app/layer-settings/layer-settings.component.ts) so the agent starts from the right examples instead of searching. Saved Codemaps can be referenced the same way (using Codemaps with the agent).
  • Open files. Files open in the editor are visible to the agent. Open view-model.ts, sidebar.component.html and the layer-settings component before you prompt in Part 2.
  • Images. Paste a screenshot or mockup into the input. You will do this in 3.4 to steer the report’s look.

Part 2 — Plan the feature Desktop 101~15 min

Devin Local has three agent modes: Code (full tools), Plan (read-only research that ends in a written plan you approve) and Ask (questions and answers, search tools only). Switch with the mode selector under the input, or by typing /ask, /plan and /normal, the same slash commands the CLI uses (mode switching). The default pattern for the rest of the lab: open in Plan mode, agree the plan, then let the agent move into Code mode. Starting in Code mode is for changes small enough that a plan would be longer than the diff.

2.1 — Pick a model

The model selector sits beside the input. Use whichever model your organisation has provisioned for FedRAMP. A stronger reasoning model helps in Plan mode; a faster one is fine for the edits in Part 3.

2.2 — Ask mode: confirm the patterns

Ask mode is a read-only conversation with no edits and no shell, so it is a cheap way to test your understanding before you commit to a plan (modes). Switch to Ask and send:

Prompt Ask mode
In @nav-app/src/app, how does a sidebar panel get wired in — using layer settings as the example: the config.json feature flag, the toolbar button in the datatable component, the ViewModel sidebar state, the sidebar component's *ngIf branch, and the standalone LayerSettingsComponent with its spec? How does the ViewModel look up a TechniqueVM for a technique in a tactic, and what does TechniqueVM.annotated() consider an annotation? I want to add a per-tactic "coverage gap" report panel modelled on these patterns — which files would it touch, and which existing tests would I copy?

Compare the answer against your Codemap and use it to correct misunderstandings before they become code. If the answer does not mention that a technique VM is keyed by technique and tactic (a technique can appear under several tactics), ask a follow-up: “If the same technique appears in two tactics, does it have one TechniqueVM or two? What does that mean for counting coverage per tactic?”

2.3 — Plan mode: a repo-aware plan

Switch to Plan. The prompt below applies the 3 S’s from Desktop 101: Specific (exact behaviours and rules), Scoped (which layers, which files, what not to touch) and Structured (numbered requirements the agent can tick off):

Prompt Plan mode
Plan a "Coverage Gap report" sidebar panel for ATT&CK Navigator, modelled on the layer-settings panel. Requirements: 1. Model: in nav-app/src/app/classes add coverage-report.ts with pure types — TacticCoverage {tacticName, tacticShortname, total, annotated, percent, gaps: {techniqueID, name}[]} and CoverageReport {tactics, total, annotated, percent} — plus a coverageReportToCSV(report) helper. Export them from classes/index.ts. 2. Calculation: ViewModel.getCoverageReport(matrix): iterate every tactic in the matrix and every parent technique in tactic.techniques (Tactic already excludes revoked/deprecated). A parent counts as annotated when its own TechniqueVM.annotated() is true OR any of its sub-techniques' is. Guard with hasTechniqueVM. percent is 0–100 with one decimal; 0 when total is 0; return an empty report if the view model isn't loaded. 3. CSV: header `tactic,total,annotated,percent,gap_technique_ids`, one row per tactic, gap IDs joined with ';', a final TOTAL row, fields containing commas quoted. 4. UI: a standalone CoverageReportComponent under nav-app/src/app/coverage-report/ with @Input() viewModel, injecting DataService to find the current domain's matrix. Title "Coverage Gap Report"; a summary line "N of M techniques annotated (P%)"; a table of Tactic | Annotated / Total | % with a progress bar; clicking a tactic row expands a list of its gaps as "T1234 — Name"; an "Export CSV" button using the existing file-saver dependency, filename `_coverage.csv` (sanitise the name). 5. Wiring: add 'coverageReport' to ViewModel.sidebarContentTypes; a new *ngIf branch in sidebar.component.html; an openCoverageReport() method and a Layer Controls button (material symbol `fact_check`, tooltip "coverage gap report") in the datatable component, guarded by a new `coverage_report` feature in src/assets/config.json under layer_controls, following the existing entries. 6. Tests: a spec for the calculation (empty layer, annotated parent, annotated sub-technique only, CSV output) using the helpers in src/tests/utils/mock-data, and a component-creation spec modelled on layer-settings.component.spec.ts. Don't touch the matrix rendering, SVG export or layer-upgrade code. List every file to add or change, in order, and call out anything in the existing code that makes this harder than it looks.

Looser version: “Add a Coverage Gap report panel to the sidebar: per tactic, how many techniques are annotated vs total, which ones aren’t, and a CSV export. Model it on layer settings, include tests. Plan it.” You would then supply the sub-technique rule and the CSV shape as answers to the agent’s questions, or as corrections to its first plan.

Plan mode explores read-only, writes the plan to a Markdown file under ~/.devin/plans/ and asks for approval. Read it critically. Two things a good plan will flag: the component needs the matrix, which lives on the domain in DataService rather than on the ViewModel, so the component has to look it up via viewModel.domainVersionID; and Navigator’s ng lint target points at a removed builder, so the quality gate is Prettier plus tests. If the plan misses either, reply in Plan mode and have it revise. It should be roughly this shape:

nav-app/src/app/classes/coverage-report.ts + TacticCoverage, CoverageReport, coverageReportToCSV() nav-app/src/app/classes/coverage-report.spec.ts + calculation + CSV tests nav-app/src/app/classes/index.ts export the above nav-app/src/app/classes/view-model.ts + 'coverageReport' content type, getCoverageReport(matrix) nav-app/src/app/coverage-report/ coverage-report.component.ts / .html / .scss / .spec.ts standalone panel: summary, table, expand, Export CSV nav-app/src/app/sidebar/sidebar.component.ts / .html import + *ngIf branch nav-app/src/app/datatable/data-table.component.ts / .html openCoverageReport() + toolbar button (fact_check) nav-app/src/assets/config.json + {"name": "coverage_report", "enabled": true, …}

Want a deeper plan? Include the word megaplan in your prompt. The agent asks at least one clarifying question before it writes and plans in more detail (Plan mode). Try it if your first plan was thin.

Do not approve yet. Normally you would approve here and the agent would move into Code mode. In this lab you will first write down the team’s rules (Part 3.1) and pick a permission mode (3.2) so the implementation runs under them, then come back to this conversation and approve.

Part 3 — Build it the team’s way Desktop 201~35 min

3.1 — Create AGENTS.md

AGENTS.md is a README for agents at the repo root: short, declarative rules loaded at the start of every session, for every teammate, in Devin Desktop and the CLI (and in other tools that read the same convention). A team writes down how it builds once instead of repeating it in every prompt.

The agent found the patterns on its own in Part 2, but only after you pointed it at the right files. Tomorrow a colleague opens a fresh session and asks for “a button to hide unscored techniques”. Without rules the agent may reach into DataService from a template, skip the colocated spec, run npm install and churn the lock file, or forget the config.json flag that every toolbar control has. Rules make those conventions explicit, and they are reviewed in PRs like any other code.

What goes in: the things a senior engineer tells a new hire on day one, and little else. Rules are loaded every session, so keep them short and move long procedures into Skills (Part 4).

  1. Overview: what the codebase is and how it is organised.
  2. Commands: the exact dev, format and test commands, including where they run (inside nav-app/).
  3. Conventions: the patterns the repo follows.
  4. Boundaries: what not to touch.

Draft it with the agent, in Ask mode, then edit:

Prompt Ask mode
Draft an AGENTS.md for this repo in under 40 lines: a 3-line overview, the exact commands for install, dev server, Prettier check and headless tests as run from nav-app/, the conventions (model logic in classes/ with no Angular imports, standalone components, sidebar panels wired via ViewModel.sidebarContentType, every toolbar control behind a config.json feature flag, colocated *.spec.ts, Prettier formatting), and boundaries (don't edit package-lock.json by hand, don't change the ATT&CK data loading or layer JSON format without a version bump, don't touch the Dockerfiles). Note that `ng lint` is broken upstream. Don't write the file — show me the draft.

Tighten it and save it as AGENTS.md at the repo root. Ours:

AGENTS.md# AGENTS.md — ATT&CK Navigator

## Overview
MITRE ATT&CK Navigator: an Angular + TypeScript single-page app (nav-app/) for
annotating ATT&CK matrices and saving the result as layer JSON. The model layer
is plain TypeScript in src/app/classes (ViewModel = a layer, TechniqueVM = one
technique's annotations); services load STIX data and config; components render.

## Commands (run from nav-app/)
- Install:     npm ci                       (never `npm install` — keep package-lock.json)
- Dev server:  npx ng serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 4200
- Format:      npm run prettier             (fix: npm run prettier:fix)
- Tests:       npx ng test --watch=false --browsers=ChromeHeadlessCI
- Lint:        `ng lint` references a removed builder upstream — do not "fix" it; rely on Prettier + tests.

## Conventions
- Model logic (calculations, serialisation) lives in src/app/classes and never
  imports Angular. Components call ViewModel methods; templates stay thin.
- New components are standalone (imports: [...]) and take [viewModel] as @Input.
- A sidebar panel = a value in ViewModel.sidebarContentTypes + an *ngIf branch in
  sidebar.component.html + an open…() method and button in the datatable toolbar.
- Every toolbar control is guarded by a feature in src/assets/config.json and
  checked with configService.getFeature() and isControlIncluded().
- Tests are colocated *.spec.ts (Jasmine/Karma); reuse src/tests/utils/mock-data.
  New code ships with tests. Format with Prettier before finishing.

## Boundaries
- Do not hand-edit package-lock.json or the Dockerfiles.
- Do not change how ATT&CK STIX data is loaded or the layer JSON schema
  (nav-app/src/app/classes/view-model.ts serialize/deserialize) without a
  layer-format version bump.
- Sidebar features must not modify matrix rendering or SVG export.

Start a new agent conversation so the rules load, then confirm they are active: right-click the session in the agent sidebar and choose Open customizations. AGENTS.md is listed under rules (and after Part 4, your Skills will be listed too). When the agent ignores a convention, check this view first.

3.2 — Permission modes

Devin Local separates agent modes (Code / Plan / Ask) from permission modes, which control what runs without asking (full permissions reference):

Permission modeFile editsShell / fetch / MCPUse when
Normal (default)AskAskUnfamiliar repo, sensitive work, learning the agent
Accept EditsAuto (in workspace)AskMost implementation work; you review diffs and still gate commands
BypassAutoAutoThrowaway sandboxes only; admin deny rules still apply

Switch to Accept Edits for the build (same selector as the agent mode). Edits will land without interrupting you, and every npm or npx command still shows a permission card. If a mode is not offered on your FedRAMP account, stay in Normal; it means more approval clicks and nothing else.

3.3 — Implement the plan (approve → Code mode · Accept Edits)

Back in the Part 2 conversation, approve the plan. The agent moves into implementation (Code mode); if it waits for you instead, type /normal. Follow up with the constraints below, or fold them into your approval message:

Prompt Code mode (after plan approval) · Accept Edits
Implement the approved Coverage Gap report plan. Work bottom-up: the pure types and CSV helper, then ViewModel.getCoverageReport with its spec, then the component, then the sidebar/toolbar/config wiring, then the component spec. Follow AGENTS.md. After the model layer run the coverage spec alone; at the end run `npm run prettier:fix`, then `npm run prettier`, then the full headless test suite from nav-app/, and fix anything that fails. The dev server is already running in my terminal — don't start another. Summarise what changed when you're done.

Watch the rules take effect: the calculation stays in classes/ with no Angular imports; the component is standalone with its own imports: [...]; the toolbar button is guarded by configService.getFeature('coverage_report'); the agent runs npm run prettier instead of the broken ng lint; and package-lock.json is untouched. Also watch the dev server terminal. Angular recompiles on every save, and a template typo shows up there seconds after the agent makes it.

The first headless test run needs Chrome. Karma launches ChromeHeadlessCI, which needs a Chrome or Chromium binary on the machine; Devin Desktop’s own browser does not count. If the run fails with “No binary for ChromeHeadless”, get Chrome through your software channel, or ask the agent whether CHROME_BIN can point at an existing Edge or Chromium install. If the agent tries to work around it by editing karma.conf.js, redirect it: “Leave karma.conf.js alone; tell me what binary it needs and I’ll install it.”

Review the diff one file at a time in the agent panel before you move on. The reference solution is 13 files and about 410 lines added. The interesting parts look like this:

Reference: the calculation and the CSV helper
nav-app/src/app/classes/view-model.ts (excerpt)public getCoverageReport(matrix: Matrix): CoverageReport {
    if (!this.loaded || !matrix) {
        return { tactics: [], total: 0, annotated: 0, percent: 0 };
    }

    const tactics = matrix.tactics.map((tactic) => {
        let annotated = 0;
        const gaps: { techniqueID: string; name: string }[] = [];

        for (const technique of tactic.techniques) {
            const parentAnnotated =
                this.hasTechniqueVM(technique, tactic) && this.getTechniqueVM(technique, tactic).annotated();
            const subtechniqueAnnotated = technique.subtechniques.some(
                (sub) => this.hasTechniqueVM(sub, tactic) && this.getTechniqueVM(sub, tactic).annotated()
            );

            if (parentAnnotated || subtechniqueAnnotated) annotated++;
            else gaps.push({ techniqueID: technique.attackID, name: technique.name });
        }

        gaps.sort((a, b) => a.techniqueID.localeCompare(b.techniqueID));
        const total = tactic.techniques.length;
        return {
            tacticName: tactic.name,
            tacticShortname: tactic.shortname,
            total,
            annotated,
            percent: total === 0 ? 0 : Number(((annotated / total) * 100).toFixed(1)),
            gaps,
        };
    });

    const total = tactics.reduce((sum, t) => sum + t.total, 0);
    const annotated = tactics.reduce((sum, t) => sum + t.annotated, 0);
    return { tactics, total, annotated, percent: total === 0 ? 0 : Number(((annotated / total) * 100).toFixed(1)) };
}
nav-app/src/app/classes/coverage-report.ts (excerpt)function csvField(value: string | number): string {
    const field = String(value);
    return /[",\r\n]/.test(field) ? `"${field.replace(/"/g, '""')}"` : field;
}

export function coverageReportToCSV(report: CoverageReport): string {
    const rows = ['tactic,total,annotated,percent,gap_technique_ids'];
    for (const tactic of report.tactics) {
        rows.push([
            csvField(tactic.tacticName), tactic.total, tactic.annotated, tactic.percent.toFixed(1),
            csvField(tactic.gaps.map((gap) => gap.techniqueID).join(';')),
        ].join(','));
    }
    const gaps = report.tactics.flatMap((tactic) => tactic.gaps.map((gap) => gap.techniqueID));
    rows.push([csvField('TOTAL'), report.total, report.annotated, report.percent.toFixed(1), csvField(gaps.join(';'))].join(','));
    return rows.join('\n');
}

    class="control-row-item">
    <div class="control-row-button noselect" (click)="openCoverageReport()" matTooltipPosition="below" matTooltip="coverage gap report">
        <span class="control-label" *ngIf="showControlLabels['layer']">
            {{ getControlDisplayName('layer_controls', 'coverage_report') | titlecase }}

3.4 — Steer with an image

Take a screenshot of the report panel as it renders now (or borrow the “After” picture at the top of this page), paste it into the agent input, and send:

Prompt Code mode · Accept Edits · with image
Make the coverage table look like this: tactic name left-aligned, "annotated / total" in a monospace-ish column, and the percentage followed by a thin 6px progress bar in the Navigator primary colour. Tactics at 0% should read as gaps at a glance — muted bar track, normal text. Keep the existing sidebar card styling; only change the coverage-report component's SCSS.

Images communicate spacing and hierarchy faster than text, and they work well for “make it look like this existing screen” requests.

3.5 — Interrupt and redirect

Ask for a change that spans several files, then change your mind part-way through to see how the agent handles a redirect without restarting:

Prompt Code mode · Accept Edits
Rename the sidebar content type "coverageReport" to "coverageGaps" everywhere it appears — ViewModel, sidebar template, datatable component, specs.

While it is working, type and send:

Prompt
Actually, keep "coverageReport" — revert that rename but leave everything else.

Check the final state with git status / git diff in the terminal. You should be back to coverageReport with no stray edits, and the dev server terminal should show a clean recompile.

Part 4 — Extend the agent with Skills Desktop 201~20 min

Rules and Skills are the pair from Desktop 201 that people most often mix up. Skills are reusable, on-demand procedures stored as SKILL.md files; the agent sees only their name and description until one is invoked (how Skills work). Rules (AGENTS.md) are loaded every session:

AGENTS.md (rules).devin/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
LoadedEvery session, alwaysName + description only; the full text loads when invoked (progressive disclosure)
Best forShort declarative constraints (“we do X, never Y”)Multi-step procedures, checklists, supporting scripts/templates
Invoked byNothing; it is always presentYou (/skill-name) or the agent when your request matches its description
CostPaid on every turnPaid only when used
Rule of thumbKnowledge → rulesProcess → skills

Keep AGENTS.md small and have it point at Skills for specific scenarios. Skills are committed to the repo under .devin/skills/ (where Skills live), so the whole team, and the CLI, runs the same procedure. Format reference: file structure and frontmatter. Creating a Skill is a small, well-defined edit, so this part works in Code mode directly; a plan would be longer than the change.

4.1 — Create the quality-gate Skill

A common first Skill is the set of checks a team runs before a PR. Create .devin/skills/navigator-feature-checklist/SKILL.md:

.devin/skills/navigator-feature-checklist/SKILL.md---
name: navigator-feature-checklist
description: Pre-PR quality gate for an ATT&CK Navigator change — Prettier, headless tests, config/feature-flag sanity, diff self-review.
---

Run the Navigator quality gate on the current working tree. All commands run from nav-app/.
Run every step; do not stop at the first failure — collect all findings, then fix and re-run.

1. Format:   `npm run prettier` (if it fails, run `npm run prettier:fix` and re-check)
2. Tests:    `npx ng test --watch=false --browsers=ChromeHeadlessCI`
3. Feature-flag sanity, only if the datatable toolbar changed:
   - every new control-row-item is guarded by configService.getFeature(...) and isControlIncluded(...)
   - the same feature name exists in src/assets/config.json with enabled, display_name and description
4. Diff self-review (`git diff master`): for every changed file check
   - no Angular imports in src/app/classes/*
   - new components are standalone and receive [viewModel] as an @Input
   - every new .ts under src/app has a colocated .spec.ts
   - package-lock.json is unchanged; no console.log left behind
   - user-visible strings and tooltips match the style of neighbouring controls (lower case, short)

Report a table: step | pass/fail | detail. Fix what you can, then re-run the failed steps and show the final table.

Start a fresh conversation and run it. The directory name is the identifier, so you can invoke it explicitly:

Prompt
/navigator-feature-checklist

Or implicitly: try “Is this ready for a PR?” in another conversation and watch the agent pick the Skill because your request matches its description. That matching is why the description line is the most important line in the file.

4.2 — Modify the Skill

The gate above has a gap you may have hit in Part 3: if Chrome is not available, step 2 fails for an environment reason and looks like a code failure. Ask the agent to fix the Skill:

Prompt Code mode · Accept Edits
Update .devin/skills/navigator-feature-checklist/SKILL.md: before the tests step, add a step that checks a headless Chrome/Chromium binary is available (CHROME_BIN or a default install) and, if not, reports it as an ENVIRONMENT finding with the install path to request — never by editing karma.conf.js or skipping tests silently. Also add to the self-review: "the coverage calculation treats a parent technique as annotated when any sub-technique is annotated, and revoked/deprecated techniques are excluded". Keep the file under 45 lines.

Re-run /navigator-feature-checklist. When the agent trips on the same thing twice, the fix belongs in a Skill (a procedure) or in AGENTS.md (a rule) rather than in your next prompt.

4.3 — Add a second, narrower Skill

Not every Skill is a gate. A good second Skill captures a review you would otherwise do by hand. In Navigator the riskiest thing to touch is the layer JSON format: analysts have thousands of saved layers, and the app has an upgrade path between versions.

.devin/skills/layer-format-review/SKILL.md---
name: layer-format-review
description: Review a Navigator change for impact on the layer JSON format and saved-layer compatibility — serialize/deserialize, version numbers, defaults, and the layer-upgrade path — before it is merged.
---

Review the working tree (`git diff master`) for anything that touches how a layer is saved or loaded.

Look at:
- nav-app/src/app/classes/view-model.ts serialize()/deserialize() and TechniqueVM serialize()/deserialize()
- the layer `version`/`versions` fields written by serialize(), and nav-app/src/app/layer-upgrade/*
- the sample layers under layers/ at the repo root

For each change:
- New fields: are they optional on load with a sensible default, so existing layers still open?
- Removed or renamed fields: is there an upgrade step, and was the layer format version bumped?
- Derived data (e.g. a coverage report): confirm it is computed, not persisted — the layer file must not grow a field that can be recomputed from annotations.
- Round-trip: does a layer saved by the new code load in the old code without error (ignoring the new field)?

Output: a short findings list (severity, file:line, fix) followed by "APPROVE" or "CHANGES REQUESTED".
If nothing under review touches the layer format, say so in one line and APPROVE.

Run /layer-format-review on your branch. It should conclude that the Coverage Gap report is derived from existing annotations, writes nothing new into the layer file, and approve. A “nothing to do here, and here is why” answer is the review a maintainer would otherwise do in their head.

Finally, make AGENTS.md point at the Skills so the agent uses them at the right moments. Add this to the end of the file:

AGENTS.md (append)## Skills
- Before declaring a feature done or opening a PR, run the navigator-feature-checklist skill.
- Whenever view-model.ts or technique-vm.ts serialisation changes, run the layer-format-review skill.

Open Open customizations again: both Skills now appear alongside the rules. Commit AGENTS.md and .devin/skills/ with the feature; they are part of the deliverable.

Part 5 — Verify it in the browser Desktop 101~10 min

The dev server has been recompiling on every save, so the running app at localhost:4200 already has your changes; reload the tab if the layer looks stale. First ask the agent for the click path. This makes the agent state what “done” looks like:

Prompt Ask mode
Give me the exact click path to verify the Coverage Gap report in the browser, including what I should see change after each step and how to check the exported CSV.

Then do it live:

  1. Reload localhost:4200 and create a new Enterprise ATT&CK layer. Open the Layer Controls tab of the toolbar. A new coverage gap report button (the fact_check icon) sits between the layer-settings gear and the download icon.
  2. Click it. The sidebar opens with Coverage Gap Report: 0 of 254 techniques annotated (0.0%) and 14 tactic rows all at 0 / N with empty bars. (Your exact counts depend on the current ATT&CK release.)
  3. Switch to Selection Controls, click Active Scanning in Reconnaissance, then Ctrl/Cmd-click Phishing, Disable or Modify Tools and Application Window Discovery. Open Technique Controls → scoring and type 5. The four cells turn red.
  4. Look at the panel: it now reads 4 of 254 (1.6%); Reconnaissance shows 1 / 12 · 8.3%, Initial Access 1 / 11, Defense Evasion 1 / 18, Discovery 1 / 34, and the bars have moved. No refresh is needed; the panel recalculates from the view model.
  5. Click the Reconnaissance row. It expands to list the eleven unannotated techniques as T1589 — Gather Victim Identity Information, T1590 — …, and so on. Active Scanning (T1595) is absent because it is covered. Click again to collapse.
  6. Score a sub-technique only: expand Phishing in the matrix (the small arrow), clear the parent’s score, and score just Spearphishing Attachment. Initial Access stays at 1 / 11, because a parent counts as covered when any sub-technique is.
  7. Click Export CSV. Your browser downloads layer_coverage.csv (the layer is called “layer” until you rename it in layer settings). Open it: header tactic,total,annotated,percent,gap_technique_ids, one row per tactic with the gap IDs joined by ;, and a final TOTAL row.

5.1 — Break it on purpose, fix it from the terminal

The agent can read your terminal as well as your files. Open nav-app/src/app/coverage-report/coverage-report.component.html and misspell the method in the summary line (for example getReprt().annotated). Save. The dev-server terminal prints an Angular template error (Property 'getReprt' does not exist on type 'CoverageReportComponent') and the browser shows the red error overlay. Then ask:

Prompt Code mode · Accept Edits
The app stopped compiling — read the ng serve output in my terminal and fix it.

The agent reads the error, traces it to the template and fixes it. You can also highlight the error in the terminal and press Cmd/Ctrl+L to send only that selection. This is the everyday loop: run it, let the agent read the terminal, fix from the real error.

Part 6 — Stretch: layer comparison from the CLI CLI 101~30–45 min

Everything you did in Devin Desktop is available in the Devin CLI: the same agent harness, AGENTS.md, Skills and modes. This part uses a second, harder feature to show it: a coverage diff between two layers (“what did we cover this quarter that we did not last quarter?”). Load a second layer, compute both reports, and show per-tactic deltas with newly covered and newly exposed techniques. There is no reference solution for this one. You plan and build it with the CLI the way you did in Desktop.

6.1 — Start a session and prove the shared config

cd path/to/attack-navigator      # the same checkout
devin                            # opens the interactive REPL
/login                           # first time only — opens a browser to authenticate

Inside the REPL, type / and scroll the command list, then check what loaded:

/navigator-feature-checklist

Your Skill runs unchanged from the terminal. The CLI found .devin/skills/ and AGENTS.md the same way Desktop did, with nothing to copy or configure.

6.2 — Plan mode from the terminal

Same habit as Desktop: plan first. Switch to Plan mode with /plan (Shift+Tab cycles modes; see CLI modes) and send:

CLI prompt /plan
Plan a "compare coverage" feature building on the Coverage Gap report on this branch, following AGENTS.md: in the report panel, a "Compare with…" control that lists the other open layers of the same domain (ViewModelsService has them); when one is chosen, compute both reports and show per tactic: baseline %, current %, delta, plus two expandable lists — techniques newly covered and techniques newly exposed (covered in the baseline, not now). Extend the CSV export with baseline/delta columns when a comparison is active. Pure diff logic in classes/ with a spec; no changes to the layer JSON format. List files in order and flag risks.

The plan file lands under ~/.devin/plans/; open it in Devin Desktop if you prefer reading there. Approve when it is right, and the agent returns to Normal mode to implement.

6.3 — Build in Accept Edits

Before approving, pick the permission mode for the build, the same choice you made in 3.2:

/accept-edits
CLI prompt accept-edits
Implement the approved plan bottom-up, running the relevant spec after each layer from nav-app/. When you're done, run the layer-format-review skill and then the navigator-feature-checklist skill, and address their findings before reporting back.

Shell commands still prompt (press Enter to approve, or type feedback to redirect); edits apply. To run something yourself without leaving the session, prefix it with ! (running shell commands):

!git status
!cd nav-app && npm run prettier

6.4 — Manage the context window

After a plan and a multi-layer build, the session is carrying a lot of history. Check, then compact at a natural breakpoint:

/context      # how much of the context window this session has used, and by what
/compact      # summarise the conversation and continue with the essentials carried forward

Use /clear when you want to start fresh instead (session management commands). Compact when you are continuing the same task; clear when you switch tasks.

6.5 — Connect one MCP server

MCP servers give the agent external tools. For a web app, the most useful is a browser the agent can drive to check its own work, which the Playwright MCP provides. From another terminal in the repo (adding servers via the command line; you have Node from Part 0, so npx is available):

devin mcp add playwright -- npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest
devin mcp list

By default the server is saved to the local scope (a gitignored file under .devin/); use -s project to share it with the team, or -s user for all your projects (MCP configuration). Devin Local prompts before the first call to any MCP tool; allow it for the session. Then, back in the REPL:

CLI prompt
Use the playwright MCP to open http://localhost:4200, create an Enterprise ATT&CK layer, score two techniques in different tactics, open the coverage gap report from Layer Controls, and confirm the summary reads "2 of N techniques annotated" and that exactly two tactic rows are non-zero. Report what you saw with a screenshot.

Check both MCP lists. Rules and Skills are shared between Devin Local in Desktop and the CLI because they live in the repo. MCP servers are also scoped config files (project, local, user), but the CLI and Devin Desktop document different file names. After devin mcp add, open the Devin Local MCP list in Devin Desktop and, if Playwright is not there, add it from that UI too (Devin Local: MCP server configuration). If your network policy blocks npx package downloads, skip this step; the rest of the lab does not depend on it.

6.6 — Wrap up

Commit both features with AGENTS.md and .devin/skills/ on your branch. Whether you open a PR against a fork is up to your team. You now have a repo where the next engineer’s agent starts with your conventions loaded.

FAQ & gotchas

Setup

npm ci fails with a certificate / proxy error. Corporate networks often need npm config set proxy … / https-proxy and a CA bundle (cafile). Ask IT for the standard settings for your machine rather than setting strict-ssl=false.

The matrix stays empty after “Create New Layer”. Navigator fetches ATT&CK STIX data from MITRE’s GitHub (raw.githubusercontent.com). If that’s blocked, download the Enterprise STIX bundle where you can, drop it under nav-app/src/assets/, and point the versions entry in src/assets/config.json at the local file. USAGE.md documents the keys. This is a good Plan-mode task for the agent.

Tests fail with “No binary for ChromeHeadless”. Karma needs Chrome or Chromium on the machine. Install Chrome through your software channel, or set CHROME_BIN to an existing Chromium-based browser (Edge works on Windows). Do not edit karma.conf.js for this.

npm run lint / ng lint fails with “Cannot find builder … tslint”. Known upstream issue: the project’s angular.json still references the removed TSLint builder. It is out of scope for this lab, where the quality gate is Prettier plus tests. Migrating to ESLint would be a separate change, and a reasonable Plan-mode exercise.

Port 4200 already in use. Stop the other process or pass --port 4300 to ng serve.

Do I need Docker? No. The Dockerfiles in the repo are for hosting Navigator; local development is Node only.

Devin Desktop & CLI

Devin Local vs Cascade? Devin Desktop has two local agents. Devin Local is the primary one and shares its harness with the CLI (same modes, permissions, Skills format, MCP config). Cascade is the earlier agent with its own settings. This lab uses Devin Local so that what you learn carries over to the terminal.

The agent ignored a rule. Check Open customizations to see whether AGENTS.md is listed. Rules load at session start, so start a new conversation after editing them. Then make the rule shorter and more concrete; long rule files get skimmed.

The agent did not pick my Skill automatically. Improve the description, which is the only part the agent sees until it invokes the Skill. Or invoke it explicitly with /skill-name.

A mode from the slides is not offered. Some modes are disabled in the FedRAMP boundary or roll out gradually. Normal, Accept Edits, Plan and Ask cover everything in this lab.

What is in scope in FedRAMP? This lab uses Devin Desktop (Tab, DeepWiki, Codemaps, Devin Local, Rules, Skills, MCP) and the Devin CLI. Cloud-hosted features shown in other material are not required here. See docs.devin.ai/federal.

Something broke in Devin Desktop itself. Command Palette → Download Devin Logs File and include it when you report to your admin; JetBrains users also attach idea.log.

The feature

Why count a parent as covered when only a sub-technique is annotated? Because that is how analysts read the matrix: the parent cell shows (1/4) and takes the colour of its children. Reporting the parent as a gap would contradict what the user sees. The CSV keeps the rule explicit so a downstream consumer can apply a different one.

Why compute the report on the view model instead of storing it in the layer? It is derived data. Anything that can be recomputed from annotations should not be persisted, or saved layers drift out of sync with themselves. This is what the layer-format-review Skill checks for.

Why a feature flag in config.json? Every Navigator toolbar control has one, so organisations hosting a customised Navigator can hide features. Following the convention means your panel can be turned off the same way as everything else, and the rule in AGENTS.md means the next feature will follow it too.

Why does the same technique count in several tactics? A technique can belong to multiple tactics (e.g. Valid Accounts is Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation and Defense Evasion), and Navigator keeps one TechniqueVM per technique-tactic pair. The report follows that model: per-tactic numbers are exact, and the TOTAL row sums cells, not unique techniques.
